You are required to complete Part 1 of the document. Part 2 is left in place for your reference, but you should only complete part 1 at this time. Please upload a document to address the written requirements. You will post your document here in the discussions page. Please comment on at least 4 other student's project reports. The document is worth 100 points.

I would like for you to make a video where you discuss your project and cover the material from your document. The video is worth 50 points.

Many thanks to Tiffany Thiessen and her team for creating this template.

 

Additional notes from the syllabus:

Project 1

 

The big push this project is for you to really think through what you are going to do this semester to add something to your resume. If you can get it done in a single page, cool. If it takes you 50 pages, I understand. There is no example length. The good students that are really working on something cool usually have more than 2 pages, because they have lots of cool links that they want to work through that will help them with their project. The uninteresting projects can be done in less than a page.

This week you are making the plan. You are giving the things you will work through and spelling out when you will work through them. You are explaining why this matters to you. I would suggest you try to articulate why it matters to an employer as well.

For picking a project, there are no bad answers. If you do something you love, I would tell you to keep doing that. If you do something you hate, now you know to never do it again. If you pick something related to programming, you will have many friends in the class. If you do something outside of programming, you might have to look farther to find someone to work with you.

I left the requirements broad. This means that about anything you turn in I can count for full credit. The goal is to give you the freedom to choose something that will benefit you and your career. Unfortunately, in order to be able to accept a broad range of styles and career goals from all students, it is difficult to pin down what needs to be done. In the past, I have looked for reasons to give people full credit. I have accepted less than stellar work because they showed effort. This assignment is a pass fail grade, and I pass most anything. This assignment was never about a grade. Unfortunately, the grade is the only way I can get people to make sure they make time to do it. The push behind this is to help you do well on something you believe will benefit you.

The other thing that makes this a hard assignment is that not everyone has given thought to what their career should look like. It is hard to start to develop a skill set to support a career that does not exist.

I am sorry this is challenging. My goal is to help you become familiar with the big challenges of life, such as thinking about your future and owning the preparation process for it. It is my hope that as you become more familiar with these questions, you will be less stressed by them when the test of life comes your way.

Good luck friend. What you do with that freedom is up to you. I hope this helps.

For my finals, I ask you to answer a few reflection questions. I am asking you to do five. You are welcome to answer as many as you need, and to share other reflections if you like. But I would like to see you pick 5 and go from there. Here is a link to the questions. I will also paste them in down below.

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1m3XZ5IFSUxRBs_P2B1-Q-qwn2i3ioebpTxWNcDMBAAs/edit?usp=sharing (Links to an external site.)

I ask that you pick your favorite 5 questions to answer. These are pass/fail, so any answer is acceptable. Feel free to take as much time as you need, and use any resources you like.

I also ask that you share a favorite meme or quote or something that stands out to you personally.

If we have a scheduled time to meet for a final, I will be in the room at that time, and you are welcome to join me, but you are not required to make an appearance. An online file submission is fine.

Thank you for all your hard work this semester.

Respectfully,

Jeremy

 

 

The final will be graded pass fail. You get full credit for any answer you give, as long as you give an answer. You may get bonus points for great answers. These are open book, open note, open internet, call a friend or family member questions. Take as much time as you like, and feel free to resubmit if you change your mind later.

Pick your favorite five questions to answer (5 or more)

And if you have a question you would rather talk about, please tell me what that question is and then answer that question.

and

please share your most relatable meme after completing this semester.

 

  1. How were you able to help others during the semester?
  2. What can I do as a faculty, through the syllabus, as well as my own behavior, to encourage the types of behavior you want to see in yourself to make you a better classmate?
  3. Explain the greatest opportunity you took advantage of this semester.
  4. What steps did you take this semester towards your career this semester and explain why it was important to you.
  5. Describe the area that you showed the most personal growth in during this class and explain what helped you make that improvement.
  6. Explain what your favorite assignment was and why it was your favorite.
  7. If you could award a prize to a classmate or someone outside of class, what would it be and why?
  8. Describe your best tools for getting the support you needed for this class.
  9. What was your favorite non-school activity from this semester?

Chipotle
12
cars

#1) 2.13 LAB: Driving costs

Video on how to work through with Jupyter Notebook: https://youtu.be/0VEsQkW6Rx8

Video featuring Jordan Benites working through this problem but doing cost of snacks for gaming instead: https://youtu.be/rBIWxvxjfGs

Driving is expensive. Write a program with a car's miles/gallon and gas dollars/gallon (both floats) as input, and output the gas cost for 20 miles, 75 miles, and 500 miles.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print('{:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f}'.format(your_value1, your_value2, your_value3))

Ex: If the input is:

20.0
3.1599
Then the output is:

3.16 11.85 79.00

#2) 2.16 LAB: Musical note frequencies

video on how to work the problem:

https://youtu.be/gf_jfABaIoo

On a piano, a key has a frequency, say f0. Each higher key (black or white) has a frequency of f0 * r^n, where n is the distance (number of keys) from that key, and r is 2^(1/12). Given an initial key frequency, output that frequency and the next 4 higher key frequencies.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print('{:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f}'.format(your_value1, your_value2, your_value3, your_value4, your_value5))

Ex: If the input is:

440
(which is the A key near the middle of a piano keyboard), the output is:

440.00 466.16 493.88 523.25 554.37
Note: Use one statement to compute r = 2^(1/12) using the pow function (remember to import the math module). Then use that r in subsequent statements that use the formula fn = f0 * r^n with n being 1, 2, 3, and finally 4.

#3) 19.7 LAB: Square root

video on one way to solve the problem: https://youtu.be/mshybBCyDw0

Given a floating-point number as input, output the square root of the given number.

Hint: Use the appropriate function from the math module to perform the operation.

Ex: If the input is:

9.0
the output is:

Sqrt: 3.0

    binary_string = str(string_reverse(binary_string))
    
    print(binary_string)

Complete the Car class by creating an attribute purchase_price (type int) and the method print_info() that outputs the car's information.

2011
18000
2018

where 2011 is the car's model year, 18000 is the purchase price, and 2018 is the current year, then print_info() outputs:

  Purchase price: $18000

    def __init__(self):
        self.model_year = 0
        # TODO: Declare purchase_price attribute
      
        self.current_value = 0

        depreciation_rate = 0.15
        # Car depreciation formula
        car_age = current_year - self.model_year
        self.current_value = round(self.purchase_price * (1 - depreciation_rate) ** car_age)
    
    # TODO: Define print_info() method to output model_year, purchase_price, and current_value


if __name__ == "__main__":    
    year = int(input()) 
    price = int(input())
    current_year = int(input())

    my_car.model_year = year
    my_car.purchase_price = price

Water

the output is:

  Carbohydrates: 0.00 g
  Protein: 0.00 g

M&M's
10.0
34.0
2.0
3.0

  Fat: 10.00 g
  Carbohydrates: 34.00 g
  Protein: 2.00 g
Number of calories for 1.00 serving(s): 234.00
Number of calories for 3.00 serving(s): 702.00

    # TODO: Define constructor with arguments to initialize instance 
    #       attributes (name, fat, carbs, protein)
       
    def get_calories(self, num_servings):
        # Calorie formula
        calories = ((self.fat * 9) + (self.carbs * 4) + (self.protein * 4)) * num_servings;
        return calories

        print(f'Nutritional information per serving of {self.name}:')
        print(f'  Fat: {self.fat:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Carbohydrates: {self.carbs:.2f} g')
        print(f'  Protein: {self.protein:.2f} g')

        amount_fat = float(input())
        amount_carbs = float(input())
        amount_protein = float(input())
        num_servings = float(input())

        food_item.print_info()
        print(f'Number of calories for {1.0:.2f} serving(s): {food_item.get_calories(1.0):.2f}')
        print(f'Number of calories for {num_servings:.2f} serving(s): {food_item.get_calories(num_servings):.2f}')

Many thanks to Tiffany Thiessen and her team for creating this template.

 

Additional notes from the syllabus:

Project 1

 

The big push this project is for you to really think through what you are going to do this semester to add something to your resume. If you can get it done in a single page, cool. If it takes you 50 pages, I understand. There is no example length. The good students that are really working on something cool usually have more than 2 pages, because they have lots of cool links that they want to work through that will help them with their project. The uninteresting projects can be done in less than a page.

This week you are making the plan. You are giving the things you will work through and spelling out when you will work through them. You are explaining why this matters to you. I would suggest you try to articulate why it matters to an employer as well.

For picking a project, there are no bad answers. If you do something you love, I would tell you to keep doing that. If you do something you hate, now you know to never do it again. If you pick something related to programming, you will have many friends in the class. If you do something outside of programming, you might have to look farther to find someone to work with you.

I left the requirements broad. This means that about anything you turn in I can count for full credit. The goal is to give you the freedom to choose something that will benefit you and your career. Unfortunately, in order to be able to accept a broad range of styles and career goals from all students, it is difficult to pin down what needs to be done. In the past, I have looked for reasons to give people full credit. I have accepted less than stellar work because they showed effort. This assignment is a pass fail grade, and I pass most anything. This assignment was never about a grade. Unfortunately, the grade is the only way I can get people to make sure they make time to do it. The push behind this is to help you do well on something you believe will benefit you.

The other thing that makes this a hard assignment is that not everyone has given thought to what their career should look like. It is hard to start to develop a skill set to support a career that does not exist.

I am sorry this is challenging. My goal is to help you become familiar with the big challenges of life, such as thinking about your future and owning the preparation process for it. It is my hope that as you become more familiar with these questions, you will be less stressed by them when the test of life comes your way.

Good luck friend. What you do with that freedom is up to you. I hope this helps.

Many thanks to Tiffany Thiessen and her team for creating this template.

 

Additional notes from the syllabus:

Project 1

 

The big push this project is for you to really think through what you are going to do this semester to add something to your resume. If you can get it done in a single page, cool. If it takes you 50 pages, I understand. There is no example length. The good students that are really working on something cool usually have more than 2 pages, because they have lots of cool links that they want to work through that will help them with their project. The uninteresting projects can be done in less than a page.

This week you are making the plan. You are giving the things you will work through and spelling out when you will work through them. You are explaining why this matters to you. I would suggest you try to articulate why it matters to an employer as well.

For picking a project, there are no bad answers. If you do something you love, I would tell you to keep doing that. If you do something you hate, now you know to never do it again. If you pick something related to programming, you will have many friends in the class. If you do something outside of programming, you might have to look farther to find someone to work with you.

I left the requirements broad. This means that about anything you turn in I can count for full credit. The goal is to give you the freedom to choose something that will benefit you and your career. Unfortunately, in order to be able to accept a broad range of styles and career goals from all students, it is difficult to pin down what needs to be done. In the past, I have looked for reasons to give people full credit. I have accepted less than stellar work because they showed effort. This assignment is a pass fail grade, and I pass most anything. This assignment was never about a grade. Unfortunately, the grade is the only way I can get people to make sure they make time to do it. The push behind this is to help you do well on something you believe will benefit you.

The other thing that makes this a hard assignment is that not everyone has given thought to what their career should look like. It is hard to start to develop a skill set to support a career that does not exist.

I am sorry this is challenging. My goal is to help you become familiar with the big challenges of life, such as thinking about your future and owning the preparation process for it. It is my hope that as you become more familiar with these questions, you will be less stressed by them when the test of life comes your way.

Good luck friend. What you do with that freedom is up to you. I hope this helps.

Programming Assignment

#1) 2.13 LAB: Driving costs

Video on how to work through with Jupyter Notebook: https://youtu.be/0VEsQkW6Rx8

Video featuring Jordan Benites working through this problem but doing cost of snacks for gaming instead: https://youtu.be/rBIWxvxjfGs

Driving is expensive. Write a program with a car's miles/gallon and gas dollars/gallon (both floats) as input, and output the gas cost for 20 miles, 75 miles, and 500 miles.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print('{:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f}'.format(your_value1, your_value2, your_value3))

Ex: If the input is:

20.0
3.1599
Then the output is:

3.16 11.85 79.00

#2) 2.16 LAB: Musical note frequencies

video on how to work the problem:

https://youtu.be/gf_jfABaIoo

On a piano, a key has a frequency, say f0. Each higher key (black or white) has a frequency of f0 * r^n, where n is the distance (number of keys) from that key, and r is 2^(1/12). Given an initial key frequency, output that frequency and the next 4 higher key frequencies.

Output each floating-point value with two digits after the decimal point, which can be achieved as follows:
print('{:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f} {:.2f}'.format(your_value1, your_value2, your_value3, your_value4, your_value5))

Ex: If the input is:

440
(which is the A key near the middle of a piano keyboard), the output is:

440.00 466.16 493.88 523.25 554.37
Note: Use one statement to compute r = 2^(1/12) using the pow function (remember to import the math module). Then use that r in subsequent statements that use the formula fn = f0 * r^n with n being 1, 2, 3, and finally 4.

#3) 19.7 LAB: Square root

video on one way to solve the problem: https://youtu.be/mshybBCyDw0

Given a floating-point number as input, output the square root of the given number.

Hint: Use the appropriate function from the math module to perform the operation.

Ex: If the input is:

9.0
the output is:

Sqrt: 3.0

4.18 LAB: Leap year

Example Video: https://youtu.be/hG_Jxiv0kAM
A year in the modern Gregorian Calendar consists of 365 days. In reality, the earth takes longer to rotate around the sun. To account for the difference in time, every 4 years, a leap year takes place. A leap year is when a year has 366 days: An extra day, February 29th. The requirements for a given year to be a leap year are:

1) The year must be divisible by 4

2) If the year is a century year (1700, 1800, etc.), the year must be evenly divisible by 400

Some example leap years are 1600, 1712, and 2016.

Write a program that takes in a year and determines whether that year is a leap year.

Ex: If the input is:

1712

the output is:

1712 - leap year

Ex: If the input is:

1913

the output is:

1913 - not a leap year

video on a possible way to work this problem: https://youtu.be/qFbsWvsWBf0
Golf scores record the number of strokes used to get the ball in the hole. The expected number of strokes varies from hole to hole and is called par (i.e. 3, 4, or 5). Each score's name is based on the actual strokes taken compared to par:
  • "Eagle": number of strokes is two less than par

6

    binary_val = ''

            binary_val += '1'

    reverse_input = ''
    
    for i in range(len(input_string)-1, -1, -1): 
        reverse_input += input_string[i]

    binary_string = str(int_to_reverse_binary(user_input))
    binary_string = str(string_reverse(binary_string))
    
    print(binary_string)
